name: MSP432E401YTPDT
title: SimpleLink Ethernet microcontroller, 120 MHz Arm Cortex-M4F, 1024 KB flash, 10/100 Ethernet MAC and PHY
summary: MSP432E401Y is a 32-bit microcontroller on a 120 MHz Arm Cortex-M4F with floating point, 1024 KB flash, 256 KB SRAM and 6 KB EEPROM. It carries a 10/100 Ethernet MAC with an on-chip PHY and IEEE 1588 timestamping, USB 2.0 OTG with a ULPI port, eight UARTs, four quad-SSI, ten I2C and two CAN controllers, two 2 Msps 12-bit ADCs, three comparators, an 8-output PWM, a parallel external peripheral interface, AES, DES, SHA/MD5 and CRC engines, and a battery-backed hibernation module with RTC and tamper inputs. It runs from 2.97 V to 3.63 V, makes its 1.2 V core supply with an internal LDO, and comes in a 128-pin TQFP rated –40°C to 105°C.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M4F with FPU, 120 MHz, 150 DMIPS

circuits.description: An external reference source drives the ADC reference pins. VREFA+ carries the positive side and GNDA the negative side, which may be grounded. The reference is selected by setting the VREF field of ADCCTL to 0x1, and its noise across the pins must stay below 12-bit full scale (–74 dB).

operation.text: MSP432E401Y is a SimpleLink Ethernet microcontroller built on a 120 MHz Arm Cortex-M4F with FPU, 1024 KB flash, 256 KB SRAM and 6 KB EEPROM, a 10/100 Ethernet MAC with its own PHY, USB 2.0 OTG, and a 128-pin TQFP (PDT) package rated –40°C to 105°C ambient. It is code compatible with the rest of the SimpleLink family through the SimpleLink SDK.

Cortex-M4F core: 150 DMIPS at 120 MHz, Thumb-2 mixed 16/32-bit instructions, single-cycle multiply, hardware divide, bit-banding, unaligned access, saturating arithmetic and a 16-bit SIMD unit. Harvard buses, an MPU, and serial wire debug and trace.
A 24-bit down counter that clears on write and wraps at zero, for an RTOS tick, alarms or time measurement.

The NVIC handles 7 system exceptions and 109 interrupts at 8 priority levels. Entry takes 12 cycles, or 6 with tail-chaining (no FPU stacking). An external NMI input is provided. Vector numbers and addresses are in the interrupt table.

IEEE 754 single precision: add, subtract, multiply, divide, fused multiply-accumulate and square root, fixed/float conversions, denormals and all rounding modes; 32 single-precision registers (also 16 doubles); 3-stage pipeline.
Arm PMSA memory protection with overlapping regions, access permissions and memory attributes.
256 KB at 0x2000.0000 in four interleaved 32-bit banks, almost 2 GB/s at 120 MHz. Bit-band aliases give atomic bit access. The µDMA, USB and Ethernet controller can master SRAM transfers.

1024 KB as four 256 KB banks of 16K × 128 bits, two-way interleaved. Blocks can be marked read-only or execute-only for code protection. Two prefetch buffers of 2 × 256 bits, combinable into one 4 × 256-bit buffer. The µDMA can read flash in run mode. 100 000 program/erase cycles; 20 years retention at TJ = 85°C.
The internal ROM at 0x0100.0000 holds the SimpleLink SDK peripheral driver library and a bootloader for in-field firmware updates.

6 KB as 1536 32-bit words in 96 blocks of 16 words, with wear leveling, per-block access protection, lock protection by 32- to 96-bit unlock codes, and a write-complete interrupt. Endurance per 2-page block runs from 500k writes (fixed offset, alternate pages, circular) to 15M operations (cycling two pages).

A 4 GB space in eight 512 MB zones: code from 0x0000.0000, SRAM from 0x2000.0000, peripherals from 0x4000.0000, EPI-mapped external RAM and devices from 0x6000.0000 to 0xDFFF.FFFF, and the private peripheral bus from 0xE000.0000. The peripheral addresses are in the memory map table.

An 8-, 16- or 32-bit parallel bus with a write FIFO, blocking and non-blocking reads, and µDMA channels for read and write. SDRAM mode: ×16 single-data-rate SDRAM up to 60 MHz and 64 MB (512 Mb), auto refresh, sleep mode, multiplexed address and data. Host-bus mode: ×8 and ×16 MCU-style buses for SRAM, NOR flash and other devices, 1 MB addressing non-multiplexed and 256 MB multiplexed (512 MB in host-bus 16 without byte selects), PSRAM up to 512 Mb in quad chip-select mode, muxed or demuxed address and data, external FIFO support, wait states, bursts, single, dual or quad chip selects, and an iRDY stall input. General-purpose mode: up to 32 data bits at up to 150 MB/s for CPLDs and FPGAs, with optional 4- to 20-bit address, clock, strobes and framing. It can also act as 1 to 32 bits of FIFO-backed parallel GPIO.

Computes CRC16-CCITT, CRC16-IBM, CRC32-IEEE and CRC32C, fed by words or bytes from code, flash or µDMA, with automatic or manual initialization, MSb or LSb first and CCITT post-processing. Works with the AES and DES modules.
Hardware AES with 128-, 192- and 256-bit keys and key scheduling: ECB, CBC, CTR, CFB-128, F8, XTS, GCM with GHASH, CCM, CBC-MAC and F9 authentication, with µDMA support.
Hardware DES and 3DES in ECB, CBC and CFB modes, driven by interrupt or µDMA.
Hardware MD5, SHA-1, SHA-224 and SHA-256 hashing and HMAC, with HMAC keys of 64 bytes or less preprocessed automatically, µDMA transfers and a digest-ready interrupt.

An IEEE 802.3 10BASE-T/100BASE-TX MAC with integrated PHY: full or half duplex, flow control, auto-negotiation, VLAN tag detection, IEEE 1588-2002/2008 timestamping with a pulse-per-second output, four MAC address filters, a 64-bit multicast hash filter, checksum offload for IPv4, IPv6, TCP, UDP and ICMP, RMON/MIB counters, magic-packet wake, its own descriptor DMA, MDI/MDI-X crossover, programmable transmit amplitude and automatic polarity correction. With the PHY in use the main oscillator reference is 25 MHz. RBIAS needs 4.87 kΩ, 1 % to ground. MAC alone adds 1.9 mA, MAC and PHY 30 mA at 120 MHz.

Two CAN 2.0A/B controllers up to 1 Mbps, each with 32 message objects with their own identifier masks, FIFO mode, loopback test mode and a no-retransmission mode for time-triggered CAN. They connect to an external transceiver through CANnTx and CANnRx.

One USB 2.0 controller as device, host or OTG. Full speed uses the integrated PHY; high speed (480 Mbps) needs an external PHY on the ULPI port. Link power management, all four transfer types, 16 endpoints (control IN and OUT plus 7 IN and 7 OUT), 4 KB endpoint memory, VBUS droop detection and its own DMA. The system clock is at least 30 MHz with MOSC as its source while USB runs. PB1 (USB0VBUS) is the one 5 V tolerant pin.

Eight 16C550-like UARTs (not register compatible) up to 7.5 Mbps at divide-by-16 or 15 Mbps at divide-by-8, with 16-byte TX and RX FIFOs, IrDA SIR up to 115.2 kbps, ISO 7816 smart card support, 9-bit EIA-485 and µDMA. UART0 and UART1 have full modem flow control and status lines; UART2 to UART4 have flow control only. The baud clock comes from SYSCLK or ALTCLK.

Ten I2C modules, each master and slave at once, at 100 kbps, 400 kbps, 1 Mbps and 3.33 Mbps (high speed), with 8-entry RX and TX FIFOs, glitch suppression, SMBus support in software, multi-master arbitration, 7-bit addressing and µDMA. Each SCL output has an active pullup, so its pin is not set to open drain.

Four synchronous serial modules, master or slave, in Freescale SPI or TI SSI framing in legacy mode and Freescale framing in bi- and quad-SSI modes. Frames of 4 to 16 bits, 16-bit × 8 TX and RX FIFOs, loopback test mode and µDMA. As master the system clock is at least twice SSIClk; as slave at least 12 times.

An Arm PrimeCell 32-channel controller moving data between memory and peripherals or memory and memory in basic, ping-pong and scatter-gather modes, two priority levels, 8-, 16- or 32-bit data, 1 to 1024 transfers per request and a completion interrupt per channel. Each channel has up to nine sources chosen by a 4-bit field in DMACHMAPn; the assignments are in the µDMA table.

The system clock comes from the 16 MHz precision oscillator (PIOSC: ±6 % from 0°C to 105°C with factory calibration, ±1 % after recalibration), the main oscillator (MOSC, a crystal across OSC0/OSC1 or a single-ended clock into OSC0), the low-frequency internal oscillator (about 33 kHz), or the hibernation RTC oscillator (32.768 kHz external or the hibernation LFIOSC), optionally through the PLL. The PLL takes 5 MHz to 25 MHz from the MOSC or the PIOSC and runs its VCO between 100 MHz and 480 MHz; it is off after power-on reset and set up through PLLFREQ0, PLLFREQ1 and RSCLKCFG, new settings taking effect when NEWFREQ is set. With the ADC running and the PLL bypassed the system clock is 16 MHz. A 128-bit unique ID identifies each device.
Power-on reset, the RST pin, brownout, software, watchdog, a hibernation event and main-oscillator failure. The internal reset time is typically 14 ms from POR release to the reset-vector fetch.

VDDA has three monitors: a power-on reset that holds the analog circuits until VDDA is usable, a power-OK that holds the digital circuits, and a brownout that resets or interrupts when VDDA falls. VDD has power-OK and brownout; VDDC has power-OK. Digital reset releases only after POR clears and every power-OK says its supply is in range. The VDD and VDDA brownouts are combined into one system brownout event: either sets the same BOR status bits (RIS, MISC, RESC) and both are controlled by BORIM in IMC and the VDDA_UBOR0 and VDD_UBOR0 bits in PWRTC.

With separate supplies VDDA comes up before VDD; the simplest arrangement ties VDDA to the VDD supply. Power-down has no ordering requirement. VDDC, made by the internal LDO, rises in 10 µs to 150 µs.

The internal LDO makes the 1.2 V VDDC core supply (1.13 V to 1.27 V in run mode, 0.9 V option in deep sleep). It needs an external filter capacitor of 2.5 µF to 4.0 µF with ESR up to 100 mΩ and ESL up to 0.5 nH, joined only to the VDDC pins and placed close to pin 115. Inrush is 50 mA to 250 mA. With the LDO at 0.9 V the system runs at no more than a quarter of full speed.

Eight 16/32-bit timer blocks, each two 16-bit timers or one 32-bit timer or 32-bit RTC: one-shot, periodic, 16-bit with 8-bit prescaler, RTC from an external 32.768 kHz clock, input edge count or time capture, and PWM with output inversion. Count up or down, daisy chaining, synchronized start, ADC triggers, debug stall and µDMA. Sixteen CCP pins do capture, compare or PWM.

Battery-backed logic that turns off the rest of the chip and wakes it on an external or timed event. It runs a 32-bit seconds RTC with a 15-bit subseconds counter (1/32768 s), a match register, predivider trim and a hardware calendar with leap-year compensation. Power is cut either by an external regulator controlled through HIB or by on-chip switches. Wake sources: the WAKE pin, RST, up to four GPIOs (port P pins can wake on level), RTC match and low battery. Four tamper inputs with level, weak pullup and glitch filter, event logging and optional battery-backed RAM erase; a failed hibernation clock switches to the internal oscillator. A 16-word (32-bit) battery-backed memory, GPIO state retention, low-battery detection. VDD powers the module whenever it is valid, even above VBAT. The clock is a 32.768 kHz crystal or oscillator on XOSC0/XOSC1, or the internal HIB LFIOSC.

Two 32-bit down-counting watchdogs: watchdog 0 runs from the system clock, watchdog 1 from the PIOSC. The first time-out can raise an interrupt or NMI and the second a reset; a lock register guards the setup, and counting can stall in debug.

Up to 90 GPIOs in 15 ports, depending on which peripherals take pins, each muxed to one of several peripheral functions by GPIOPCTL. Inputs are 3.3 V tolerant and Schmitt triggered. All ports have AHB access and can toggle every clock cycle there. Interrupts on edges or levels, per pin on ports P and Q; a GPIO can start an ADC sequence or a µDMA transfer. Pads offer weak pullup or pulldown, open drain, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 or 12 mA drive with slew control at 8 mA and above, and up to four pads can sink 18 mA. Most GPIOs are high-impedance GPIO after reset; PC0 to PC3 come up as JTAG/SWD and PD7 and PE7 come up locked.

PJ1 has the slow pad (2 mA, sensitive input); every other GPIO has the fast pad. PL6 and PL7 have fast pads fixed at 4 mA, and their drive, slew and open-drain controls do nothing. PM4 to PM7 have fast pads limited to 2, 4, 6 and 8 mA. Every I/O except PB1 is limited to 3.3 V operation; PB1 takes the 5 V USB VBUS.
The sum of source and sink current on the GPIOs of each package side is limited: left 112 mA, bottom 97.6 mA, right 112 mA, top 80 mA. The pin-to-side grouping is in the package side table.

Continuous drive at 2 mA to 12 mA between –40°C and 85°C meets a 10-year life; a continuous 18 mA sink holds 10 years only from 0°C to 75°C. At 105°C continuous drive meets 2.5 years. Switching at a 40 % rate with 50 pF loads meets 10 years at –40°C to 85°C and 2.5 years at 105°C for every drive setting except 2 mA, which needs its load cut to 20 pF to reach the same lives.

The WAKE pad has an ESD clamp to ground and no path to any supply rail; keep it within the absolute maximum ratings. Other signal pins carry a ground ESD clamp plus a diode up to their own supply; limit their voltage or current to the pad table values, and keep the ADC reference within its own limits to avoid gain error.

One PWM module with four generators and eight outputs. Each generator holds a 16-bit counter (down, or up/down), a pair of comparators, a signal generator and a dead-band generator for half-bridge pairs, and can trigger the ADC. The control block sets output enable, polarity and fault handling; four fault inputs give fast shutdown (MnFAULTn to inactive in 24 ns plus one PWM clock).

One quadrature encoder interface with phase A, phase B and index inputs, a position integrator, input noise filter and velocity capture timer, interrupting on index, velocity timer, direction change and quadrature error. Its inputs run up to a quarter of the system clock (30 MHz at 120 MHz).

Two 12-bit SAR ADCs share 20 analog inputs and an internal temperature sensor, each up to 2 Msps. Four sample sequencers of one to eight entries with result FIFOs, single-ended or differential inputs, hardware averaging up to 64 samples, a programmable phase delay and sample window, and eight digital comparators per ADC. Triggers: software, timers, comparators, PWM and GPIO. The reference is either VDDA/GNDA (VREF = 0x0) or the external VREFA+ (VREF = 0x1). Analog power and ground are separate from digital. AINx pins are configured by clearing GPIODEN and setting GPIOAMSEL. The temperature sensor gives 1.633 V at 25°C with a –13.3 mV/°C slope.

Each input sees a switch and an equivalent resistance RADC (2.5 kΩ max) into the shared sampling capacitor CADC (10 pF max), with 2.0 µA input leakage. The source resistance is at most 500 Ω at 1 Msps and 250 Ω at 2 Msps. Adjacent switching digital I/O couples into the inputs; place quiet signals next to them and band-limit neighbouring analog signals to 100 kHz.

Three comparators compare two pins, or a pin against an internal 16-step reference in two ranges, and drive a pin, raise an interrupt or trigger the ADC, with interrupt and ADC trigger on separate edges. Response time is 1 µs. While idle, hold the two inputs at different levels; in sleep or deep sleep disable the comparator or keep its inputs apart by more than the offset for lowest current.

JTAG (IEEE 1149.1) and Arm serial wire debug through one SWJ-DP, with a 4-bit instruction register, BYPASS, IDCODE, SAMPLE/PRELOAD and EXTEST, the Arm APACC, DPACC and ABORT instructions, and FPB, DWT, ITM, ETM and TPIU for breakpoints, watchpoints, printf-style output and instruction trace. TCK runs to 10 MHz. The JTAG IDCODE reads 0x4BA0.0477.

DID0 and DID1 give the version, package and temperature range; the peripheral-present registers from system control offset 0x300 count each module type; each peripheral's properties sit at offset 0xFC0 in its register space; four UNIQUEIDn registers hold a fixed 128-bit unique identifier.

After power-on reset the core loads its stack pointer and reset vector from flash when address 0x0000.0004 holds a valid vector and the EN bit of BOOTCFG is set. If that word is erased (0xFFFF.FFFF) or EN is clear, they come from ROM at 0x0100.0000 and 0x0100.0004 and the ROM bootloader waits for an image over UART0, SSI0, I2C0, USB or Ethernet. USB and Ethernet boot need an external crystal, and Ethernet boot needs it to be 25 MHz. Bootloader speed follows the PIOSC or the crystal. Because the bootloader drives some pins when flash is blank, PA1, PA4, PL6 and PL7 are not tied straight to ground.

The main oscillator takes a 4 MHz to 25 MHz crystal (5 MHz minimum with the PLL; 25 MHz with the Ethernet PHY) with 12 pF to 24 pF load capacitors per leg chosen by the load-capacitance equation, ESR from 300 Ω at 4 MHz down to 50 Ω at 25 MHz, starting within 18 ms. A series resistor Rs between OSC1 and the crystal limits drive power; the crystal table lists tested crystals with their C1, C2 and Rs. An external clock into OSC0 runs up to 120 MHz in PLL bypass with 45 % to 55 % duty; OSC1 is then left open. For Ethernet the crystal is 25 MHz within ±50 ppm, or a 25 MHz single-ended oscillator within ±50 ppm, 40 % to 60 % duty and 1 ns edges.

A 32.768 kHz crystal across XOSC0 and XOSC1 with 12 pF to 24 pF per leg; OSCDRV in HIBCTL is set for loads above 18 pF, allowing ESR up to 75 kΩ instead of 50 kΩ. Start-up takes 600 ms typical, 1500 ms maximum. A single-ended 32.768 kHz clock into XOSC0 leaves XOSC1 open. These pins are not fail-safe.

Sleep keeps the run-mode clocks, so waking costs only the LDO (39 µs), flash (96 µs) and SRAM (15 µs) restore times that apply. Deep sleep can switch to the PIOSC or the 30 kHz LFIOSC and drop the LDO to 0.9 V; restoring the MOSC then takes 18 ms and the PLL one deep-sleep clock plus 512 reference cycles. Hibernation cuts power to all but the hibernation module: about 1.2 µA from VBAT at 25°C with the RTC off, 1.29 µA with it on.

Unused GPIOs may float, or better be grounded for lower power and EMC. VREFA+ goes to VDDA, RBIAS keeps its 4.87 kΩ to ground, the Ethernet pair pins stay open. Without hibernation: VBAT to VDD, WAKE and XOSC0 to ground, HIB and XOSC1 open. An unused OSC0 goes to ground, OSC1 open. RST goes to VDD, preferably through up to 100 kΩ. Unused USB0DM/PL7 and USB0DP/PL6 are pulled down through 1 kΩ. A module whose inputs are grounded must never have its clock enabled.
